text: This chapter has covered which certifications exist, how to choose one, and how to study for it. This closing lesson steps back and asks the harder question honestly: once you pass the exam, what has it actually bought you — and just as importantly, what hasn't it bought you?

A certification demonstrates something real and specific: verified baseline knowledge against a published, standardized exam blueprint. To a recruiter scanning a stack of resumes, that's a credible, third-party-verified signal, not just a self-reported claim, and it can genuinely help clear an initial screen. That's a real benefit worth having. It is also the complete list of what a certification reliably does.

Be honest about the limits. It does not guarantee a job — relevant experience, interview performance, and fit matter at least as much. It does not guarantee a specific salary — there's no verified number any certificate entitles you to. And most importantly, it does not substitute for real hands-on project experience. It proves you can answer standardized questions correctly. It doesn't prove you can walk into a messy real organization's requirements and deliver a working implementation.

A noticeable pattern across ServiceNow hiring: employers increasingly don't take a certification at face value. They ask certified candidates to demonstrate the underlying skill directly, in a technical screen — configuring something live, or walking through a past project in real detail. The certification gets your resume a look. The technical screen is where the actual skill gets verified, and that's exactly where a resume backed by nothing but a certificate runs out of road.

That gap is precisely why this course builds a real capstone across Chapters four through six: a cumulative project, built against a realistic five-thousand-employee organization, with real requirements, real scope, real build work, and a real presentation and defense of your decisions. Certification can get your resume read. The capstone is what you'll actually be able to talk about once someone starts asking real questions. Next up, in Chapter two: what ServiceNow administrator roles actually look like in practice, in the real job market.
